hints: Look at what is happening to ventricular volume at each point. Where is it falling fast, where is it rising slowly, and where does it get a sudden extra push upwards?

Remember atrial systole is the atria contracting to push the last bit of blood into the ventricles, so look for a second, steeper rise in ventricular volume after passive filling has almost levelled off.
walkthrough:
**Read what the graph is really showing**

Think of this as watching blood enter and leave the left ventricle. When volume falls, blood is leaving. When volume rises, blood is entering.

Start volume is about $100 \text{ cm}^3$ and minimum volume is about $40 \text{ cm}^3$.

**Find ventricular systole and then passive filling**

At A the volume drops steeply from 100 to 40. That is ventricular systole, the ventricle contracting and ejecting blood into the aorta.

At B the volume is lowest and then starts to rise gradually. That is the start of ventricular diastole, when the ventricle relaxes and blood flows passively from atrium to ventricle.

**Spot the active push of atrial systole**

After B the curve rises then flattens a little. Passive filling is slowing down. Then at C there is a sudden steeper rise up to 100 again.

That extra push can only come from the atria contracting. So C is the start of atrial systole, topping up the ventricle just before the next cycle.

options.A: This is the start of ventricular systole, when the ventricle contracts and ejects blood so volume falls sharply.
options.B: This is the end of ventricular systole and start of ventricular diastole, when the ventricle relaxes and begins passive filling.
options.C: This is the start of atrial systole, when the atria contract and push a final volume of blood into the ventricle, causing the second steep rise.
options.D: This is after filling is complete, when ventricular volume is maximal and constant during late diastole.
